profile.summary_simple: NASA studied gas flames in microgravity on the ISS. Scientists burned methane and ethylene fuels with different amounts of air to learn how soot forms and how flames behave without gravity. The results help improve computer models of fire.
profile.summary_expert: The ACME Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) study ran on the ISS from September 2017 to February 2022 inside the Combustion Integrated Rack. Researchers tested methane and ethylene fuels at various dilution levels in an air coflow under microgravity. The goal was to gather benchmark data to verify chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels for sooty and extremely diluted flames. Key findings include five to eight times more soot than normal-gravity flames, taller and wider flame shapes, and wider fuel-dilution limits with more stable, lifted flames near extinction.
profile.experiment_goal: The study set out to improve computational flame models with benchmark quantitative data for sooty and extremely diluted microgravity flames.

sample_shapes: gas-jet flame with coaxial air flow

results.result_simple: Microgravity flames make much more soot than flames on Earth.
results.result_expert: Microgravity flames contain five to eight times more soot than equivalent normal-gravity flames.
results.safety_meaning: More soot in space fires means thicker smoke and harder crew evacuation.

results.result_simple: Flames in space are taller and wider than flames on Earth.
results.result_expert: Microgravity flames are taller and wider than equivalent normal-gravity flames.
results.safety_meaning: Larger flames can spread farther and threaten more equipment in a spacecraft.

results.result_simple: Diluted flames stay lit at lower fuel levels in microgravity.
results.result_expert: Microgravity increases the limits of fuel dilution for both methane and ethylene flames; near limits, microgravity flames are more stable, allowing lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations.
results.safety_meaning: Fires can persist with less fuel, so spacecraft air limits must account for very dilute flames.

equipment.note: Soot and flame-size data help tune smoke and flame detectors for microgravity conditions.
Airflow and dilution limits inform ventilation design to prevent fire spread.
Flammability limits guide material selection for spacecraft interiors.

earth_uses: improved efficiency and reduced pollution in terrestrial combustion

glossary.definition: A condition where gravity's effects are very weak, such as aboard the ISS.
